query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a machine‐learning interatomic potential, calibrated via active learning on carefully chosen ab initio free‐energy calculations (which explicitly include vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects), with an accelerated free‐energy integration scheme (such as nested interpolation), will yield high‐fidelity fusion thermodynamic properties for both liquid and solid phases in elemental, binary, and multicomponent systems while reducing computational cost by approximately one to two orders of magnitude compared to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and offering better scalability than TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent (high-entropy alloy) systems near their melting points, where both solid and liquid phases exhibit significant vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a machine-learning interatomic potential through active learning that is trained on a strategically limited set of high-fidelity ab initio free-energy calculations capturing vibrational and anharmonic contributions, and integrate it with an accelerated thermodynamic integration method (e.g., nested interpolation) to compute free energy differences.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed across a temperature range spanning the melting transition and high-temperature regimes with compositions ranging from pure elements and simple binaries to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The trained machine-learning interatomic potential acts as the surrogate for the ab initio interactions while the nested interpolation scheme serves as the accelerated method to bridge free-energy differences between phases.
generation.mechanism: The ML potential uses active learning to refine its predictions based on key ab initio data points, thereby capturing critical effects (vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, electron–vibration coupling) with minimal computational overhead. The accelerated integration scheme then efficiently evaluates the free-energy differences across phases, preserving chemical accuracy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion free energies, melting temperatures, and related entropy measures will be reproduced within chemical accuracy (e.g., mean deviations within a few meV/atom for energies) while reducing simulation times by 10–100× compared to full ab initio MD. Results should match known benchmarks for elemental and binary systems and extend reliably to multicomponent alloys.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations and the TOR-TILD method currently employed for simpler systems.
generation.boundary: Composition: from pure elements to binary systems and complex high-entropy alloys. Temperature: from just below the melting point up to high-temperature regimes where thermal excitations (vibrational and anharmonic effects) are significant.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the ML model’s ability to fully capture electron–vibration coupling in highly complex multicomponent systems and how robust the active learning strategy will be when extrapolating to regions not densely sampled in the training data.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a systematic study in which free energies and derived observables (e.g., melting temperatures, entropy differences) for a set of benchmark systems (covering elemental, binary, and multicomponent alloys near melting) are computed using the proposed ML-integrated accelerated integration method and compared against full ab initio MD results. The study should include cases at the edge of the training data to test the extrapolation capability.
measurements: Phase free energy differences for solid and liquid states
Computational time reductions relative to full MD workflows
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-integrated scheme results in free energy differences or melting point predictions that deviate beyond chemical accuracy thresholds (e.g., mean absolute error > 5 meV/atom or > a few tens of Kelvin), or if the computational cost reduction is less than one order of magnitude compared to explicit ab initio MD, then the hypothesis is falsified.

We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1. This work introduced the high-throughput phase prediction of PtPd-based high-entropy alloys via the algorithm based on a combined Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker coherent potential approximation (KKR-CPA) and artificial neural network (ANN) technique. As the first step, the KKR-CPA was employed to generate 2,720 data of formation energy and lattice parameters in the framework of the first-principles density functional theory. Following the data generation, 15 features were selected and verified for all HEA systems in each phase (FCC and BCC) via ANN. The algorithm exhibited high accuracy for all four prediction models on 36,556 data from 9139 HEA systems with 137,085 features, verified by R2 closed to unity and the mean relative error (MRE) within 5%. frame.system: Solid and liquid phases in materials undergoing fusion, specifically including elemental, binary, and multicomponent high‐entropy alloy systems where phase transitions (fusion) are examined.
frame.goal: To obtain high-fidelity free energies (and their derived thermodynamic properties) for both solid and fluid phases—including vibrational entropy, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration coupling—with a substantial reduction in computational cost compared to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and current TOR-TILD approaches.
frame.limitation: Existing approaches face excessive computational cost (explicit ab initio MD free-energy evaluation) or scalability issues (TOR-TILD slows down significantly in multicomponent high-entropy systems), making it difficult to capture all relevant fusion properties reliably.

frame.understanding: The hypothesis proposes that integrating machine-learning enhanced interatomic potentials (trained on a limited set of high-fidelity ab initio data) with advanced free-energy integration schemes (such as nested interpolation or accelerated thermodynamic integration) can replicate the necessary vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects. This hybrid approach should substantially accelerate the evaluation of free energies across both solid and liquid phases while preserving the essential physics. It is anticipated to achieve speedups by one to two orders of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio MD, and superior scalability compared to TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems. Prior success in elemental and binary system validations, where machine-learned potentials have accurately reproduced ab initio free energies, supports this approach. A decisive benchmark would be the ability of the method to reproduce phase free energy differences and derived observables (e.g., melting temperatures, entropy differences across the fusion transition) within chemical accuracy compared to full ab initio MD across a specified composition range (from pure elements up to high-entropy alloys) and temperature range (encompassing the melting and high-temperature operating regime); any systematic deviation in these benchmarks would falsify the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Early work focused on computing phase-transition temperatures using explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics and empirical potentials, which inadequately captured the full free-energy landscape (including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling). Later methods like TOR-TILD advanced throughput for simpler (elemental or binary) systems but ran into scalability issues for complex, multicomponent high-entropy alloys. Recently, frameworks have begun integrating machine-learning models (e.g., moment-tensor potentials) with ab initio data to predict thermodynamic properties efficiently, demonstrating that data-driven potentials can closely reproduce ab initio free energies in limited test cases.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how to reliably compute high-fidelity free energies (and derived fusion properties) for both the solid and liquid states in multicomponent systems while capturing subtle entropy contributions and electron–vibration interactions—all at a computational cost far below full ab initio MD and with better scalability than TOR-TILD.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning interatomic potential calibrated via active learning on a judiciously selected set of ab initio free-energy calculations (including vibrational and anharmonic contributions) and integrate it with an accelerated thermodynamic integration scheme (such as nested interpolation). Key parameters would include the size and diversity of the training dataset, error thresholds for model updates, and the stability of predicted free energies across both phase regimes near the melting point.
decision.why: This approach logically extends the trend seen in recent studies (e.g., PMC11275555) by leveraging a data-driven framework to reproduce the complex physics (vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, electron–vibration coupling) at a fraction of the cost of explicit MD. It directly addresses the high computational expense and scalability issues, offering a method that should be one to two orders of magnitude faster than ab initio MD while preserving chemical accuracy across the elemental-to-multicomponent regime.
